diagnosticQuestions.answer: Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia are both multicellular and eukaryotic, but they differ sharply in nutrition, cell structure and movement. First, the members of Kingdom Plantae are autotrophic. They contain chlorophyll and can make their own food by photosynthesis, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to form glucose and oxygen. In contrast, the members of Kingdom Animalia are heterotrophic. They cannot make their own food and must feed on plants, other animals or organic remains. Second, plant cells are surrounded by a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, which gives shape and support to the cell, while animal cells have no such cellulose wall. Third, most animals can move from one place to another at some stage of their life, whereas plants are usually fixed in the soil and show only some movement of parts. Fourth, the two kingdoms are separated at the level of organisation: both have tissue and organ systems, but the pattern of nutrition is the central dividing line. A good example of Plantae is the rose plant, which is green, has cellulose cell walls and makes its own food by photosynthesis. A good example of Animalia is the frog, which is multicellular, lacks a cell wall, catches insects for food and is capable of movement. Thus the four points, autotrophic versus heterotrophic, cellulose cell wall versus no cell wall, usually fixed versus usually mobile, and the basic mode of nutrition, clearly separate the two kingdoms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student sees an earthworm and a roundworm in the school garden. The student says they both belong to the same phylum because both are worms. Explain why this statement is only partly correct and identify the correct phylum of each organism, giving two reasons for your classification.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is only partly correct because both animals are long and cylindrical, but the word worm is not a scientific category in the ICSE syllabus. The earthworm and the roundworm are placed in different phyla because their body plans are different. The earthworm belongs to the phylum Annelida. Its body is divided into ring-like segments and it has tiny bristles called setae that help it to grip the soil and move. The roundworm, such as Ascaris, belongs to the phylum Nematoda. Its body is cylindrical and unsegmented, and it is covered by a tough protective cuticle. So, although both may look like worms to a casual observer, the presence of true body segments places the earthworm in Annelida, while the absence of segmentation and the presence of a smooth, round body places the roundworm in Nematoda. In an examination, a good answer would mention the exact phylum and at least one correct distinguishing character for each. This also shows why it is not enough to go by common names; the internal and external body features decide the phylum.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes the following statement in a test: All animals that fly are vertebrates, and all invertebrates are small, crawling animals. Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement contains two claims, and both are incorrect, so the whole statement must be rejected. First, the claim that all flying animals are vertebrates is false. While many vertebrates do fly, common examples being the sparrow, the parrot, the bat and the eagle, there are also many invertebrates that can fly. A butterfly, a honey bee, a mosquito and a housefly all have wings and are strong fliers, yet they belong to the phylum Arthropoda and have no backbone. Therefore, flight is not a sign of having a backbone; it is an adaptation found in both groups. Second, the claim that all invertebrates are small and crawling is also false. Some invertebrates, such as the garden snail and the earthworm, do crawl or glide, and they are small, but others are large and live in the sea. The octopus, a mollusc, can be very large and swims by jet propulsion; the jellyfish, a cnidarian, drifts in the water and can have a body wider than a dinner plate; and the starfish, an echinoderm, is neither small nor a crawler in the usual sense. The correct way to decide whether an animal is a vertebrate or an invertebrate is to ask whether it has a backbone. Vertebrates include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, and they belong to the phylum Chordata. Invertebrates include the eight major phyla in the syllabus, from the simple Porifera to the more complex Arthropoda and Echinodermata. So the statement confuses ability with structure and size with classification. Backbones and body-plan features, not wings or size, are the real criteria.

diagnosticQuestions.question: During a biology excursion to a beach in Odisha, a student finds a spiny-skinned animal with five arms, tube feet on the underside and no backbone. Name the phylum to which this animal belongs, give two characteristics of this phylum, name one other example of the same phylum, and state whether the animal is a vertebrate or an invertebrate with a reason.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The animal belongs to the phylum Echinodermata, because it has spiny skin, a star-shaped or radially arranged body and tube feet used for movement and feeding. Two important characteristics of Echinodermata are the presence of spiny or bumpy skin and the presence of a water-vascular system that ends in hundreds of tiny tube feet. These tube feet act like small suction cups and help the animal to crawl, attach to rocks and pull open the shells of prey. Another familiar example of Echinodermata is the sea urchin, which looks like a round, spiny ball and is also found in the sea along Indian coasts. The animal is an invertebrate because it has no backbone or vertebral column. Remember that the presence of a backbone is the simplest and most reliable test: if an animal has a bony or cartilaginous backbone, it is a vertebrate and is usually placed in the phylum Chordata, while if it lacks a backbone, it is an invertebrate and belongs to one of the many invertebrate phyla. The five-armed starfish-like animal on the Odisha beach is a clear example of an invertebrate, and its spiny skin and tube feet point directly to Echinodermata.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a one-page revision chart for a Class 7 magazine that compares a neem plant and a cockroach under the headings (i) Kingdom, (ii) Two main body characteristics, (iii) How it obtains food and (iv) One scientific name of the phylum or group to which the cockroach belongs. Write the content you would put in each section of the chart.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (i) Kingdom: The neem plant belongs to Kingdom Plantae, because it is a multicellular, eukaryotic, autotrophic organism with a cellulose cell wall. The cockroach belongs to Kingdom Animalia, because it is a multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic organism with no cellulose cell wall and is capable of movement. (ii) Two main body characteristics: The neem plant has green leaves containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis and its cells are surrounded by a cellulose wall. The cockroach has a hard, jointed body covering called an exoskeleton and three pairs of jointed legs. (iii) How it obtains food: The neem plant makes its own food by photosynthesis, using carbon dioxide, water and sunlight to produce glucose and oxygen. The cockroach cannot make its own food; it is a heterotroph and feeds on leftover food, paper, decaying matter and other organic material. (iv) Scientific group: The cockroach belongs to the phylum Arthropoda, which is the largest animal phylum and is defined by jointed legs, a chitinous exoskeleton and a segmented body. Two examples of Arthropoda common in India are the cockroach and the butterfly. The chart should therefore show that, although both organisms are living and multicellular, the plant is a self-sufficient producer while the cockroach is a consumer with a very different body plan.

masteryCriteria: Can state the main features of Plantae (multicellular, autotrophic, cell wall of cellulose) and Animalia (multicellular, heterotrophic, no cell wall); can give two examples of each kingdom; can state one difference between plants and animals at kingdom level.

title: Photosynthesis (detailed process)
subject: bio
definition:
Photosynthesis is the most important biological process on Earth because it is the way green plants make their own food. In simple words, photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to prepare glucose, a simple sugar, and release oxygen as a by-product. This food-making process takes place mainly in the leaves of the plant, though green stems can also carry it out, because leaves contain thousands of tiny, green, disc-shaped bodies called chloroplasts. Inside each chloroplast is a green pigment called chlorophyll, which is able to trap light energy from the sun.

The process can be shown as a word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(sunlight and chlorophyll)--> glucose + oxygen. This means that carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf through small openings called stomata, water is absorbed by the roots and carried up to the leaves, and in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, the two are changed into glucose and oxygen. The glucose is used by the plant as food to provide energy and to build new plant parts. Some of the glucose is converted into starch and stored in leaves and other storage organs such as potatoes, which is why a green leaf kept in sunlight tests positive for starch with iodine.

Photosynthesis is affected by four main factors. First, light intensity: more light generally means more photosynthesis, until some other factor becomes limiting. Second, carbon dioxide concentration: since carbon dioxide is a raw material, more of it in the air can speed up the process. Third, water availability: if the plant does not get enough water, photosynthesis slows down because water is needed for the reaction. Fourth, chlorophyll presence: without chlorophyll, the plant cannot capture sunlight, so it cannot photosynthesise. This is why variegated leaves, which have white or yellow patches without chlorophyll, do not produce starch in those parts.

The significance of photosynthesis is enormous. It produces the oxygen that almost all living organisms need for respiration. It makes food, directly or indirectly, for nearly every living thing on Earth, which is why green plants are called producers or autotrophs. By removing carbon dioxide and adding oxygen to the air, photosynthesis helps to keep the balance of these two gases in the atmosphere. Finally, because plants are the first organisms to make food, they form the starting point of all food chains and food webs, supporting herbivores, carnivores and decomposers alike. From the wheat fields of Punjab and Haryana to the rice paddies of West Bengal and the tea gardens of Assam, the green leaves in Indian farms and forests are quietly running this solar-powered kitchen every sunny day.
eli5: Green plants are like little cooks. They use sunlight as fire, water from the ground, and air called carbon dioxide as ingredients. With a green helper called chlorophyll inside their leaves, they cook a sweet food called glucose and give out oxygen for us to breathe. That is why we say plants are our living kitchens.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Write the word equation for photosynthesis and list the four factors that affect the process.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The word equation for photosynthesis is written as: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose + oxygen. The arrow is read as "gives" or "yields." It is important to remember that carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials, glucose and oxygen are the products, and sunlight and chlorophyll are the necessary conditions. Sunlight provides the energy for the reaction, and chlorophyll, the green pigment inside chloroplasts, captures that light energy. The four factors affecting photosynthesis are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, water availability and the presence of chlorophyll. Light intensity matters because it is the source of energy; more light usually increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a limit. Carbon dioxide concentration matters because it is one of the raw materials taken in through stomata. Water availability matters because water is the other raw material absorbed by roots and transported to leaves. Chlorophyll presence matters because without it the plant cannot trap sunlight, and photosynthesis cannot occur. The correct word equation and the correct list of four factors are the two key things the board expects in a short-answer question.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A potted plant is kept in a dark cupboard for a week. When it is taken out, its leaves have turned yellow and a starch test on the leaves gives a negative result. Explain why this happens, using your knowledge of photosynthesis.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When the potted plant is kept in a dark cupboard, it does not receive sunlight. Sunlight is one of the conditions necessary for photosynthesis, so the rate of photosynthesis falls sharply and may stop altogether. The green pigment chlorophyll in the leaves also begins to break down or fade in the absence of light, which is why the leaves lose their green colour and turn yellow. Since the plant cannot make glucose, it has no extra food to store as starch, so the starch test with iodine gives a negative result. At the same time, the plant continues to use up whatever starch it had stored for its life processes, so the amount of starch in the leaf becomes even less. This shows that both sunlight and chlorophyll are essential for photosynthesis and that starch is stored food made from glucose. Once the plant is put back in light, fresh chlorophyll can form again and photosynthesis can restart, but only if water and carbon dioxide are also available.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Plants carry out photosynthesis during the day and respiration only at night, so these two processes can never happen together in the same plant at the same time." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is partly correct but finally incorrect, so it needs to be evaluated carefully. It is true that photosynthesis in green plants takes place only in the presence of light, so it is mainly a daytime process. It is also true that, at night when there is no photosynthesis, the plant still respires, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. However, the statement that respiration occurs only at night is wrong. Respiration is a continuous, all-the-time process in living cells, both day and night, because every living cell needs energy to stay alive. During the day, while photosynthesis is going on, the plant is also respiring at the same time. The leaf makes glucose through photosynthesis and immediately uses some of it for respiration. What we observe is the net result: during the day, more oxygen is usually released than used, so a plant appears to be a source of oxygen. At night, it releases carbon dioxide because photosynthesis has stopped but respiration continues. Therefore, the two processes can and do happen together in the same plant during the day. The balanced view is that photosynthesis is light-dependent, respiration is continuous, and the difference between them is the net gas exchange, not whether they can occur at the same time. This balanced explanation is what a good Class 7 answer should show.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe an experiment you could perform with a potted plant to show that light is necessary for photosynthesis. Include the steps, the expected result and the conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To show that light is necessary for photosynthesis, take a healthy potted plant with green leaves, such as a money plant or a balsam plant, and destarch it by keeping it in a dark cupboard for two or three days. This removes any starch that is already present in the leaves. Next, cover one part of a leaf completely with black paper or aluminium foil, leaving another part of the same leaf uncovered. Place the plant in bright sunlight for about four to six hours. After that, remove the leaf, boil it in water to kill the cells and soften the leaf, then boil it in alcohol over a water bath to remove the chlorophyll. The leaf becomes pale or colourless. Wash it and test it with iodine solution. The part of the leaf that was exposed to sunlight turns blue-black, showing that starch has been formed. The part that was covered with black paper or foil does not turn blue-black, showing that no starch was made. Since starch is produced from glucose, which is made by photosynthesis, this experiment proves that light is necessary for photosynthesis. The uncovered part could carry out photosynthesis because it received light, while the covered part could not.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine your school is holding a science exhibition and you have to build a labelled model of a leaf showing how it acts as a "solar kitchen" for photosynthesis. Draw and label your model, and explain how each part is linked to the process.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In my model, I would start with a large, green, leaf-shaped board to represent the leaf. Inside it, I would attach small green discs made of paper or clay to show the chloroplasts, and I would colour them green because they contain chlorophyll. I would place small yellow dots or LED lights on the upper surface to show the stomata, the tiny openings through which carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves. A thin plastic tube running from the base of the leaf up to the middle would represent the xylem vessels carrying water from the roots. I would use a small sun cut-out or a battery-operated lamp above the leaf to show sunlight. Inside the "chloroplast" discs, I would place tiny paper cards labelled "glucose," the food, and another set of small white circles floating away from the stomata to show oxygen being released. I would label the green colour as chlorophyll, the "solar panel" that catches light. I would add arrows showing carbon dioxide going in, water coming up, sunlight shining down, and oxygen and glucose being produced. Below the model I would write the word equation and a caption: "Every green leaf is a solar kitchen: sunlight + carbon dioxide + water, with chlorophyll, makes food and oxygen." This model would clearly show the raw materials, the conditions, the site of the reaction and the products.

masteryCriteria: Can write the balanced word equation for photosynthesis (carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll); can state the role of chlorophyll and stomata; can describe one experiment to show that photosynthesis produces oxygen (hydrilla in water).

title: Respiration in plants
subject: bio
definition: Respiration in plants is the vital biochemical process by which a plant breaks down food, mainly the sugar glucose, to release energy that powers every living activity of the organism. Unlike the simple mechanical movement of air in and out of the body that we call breathing, respiration is a chemical breakdown that happens inside cells, especially within tiny organelles called mitochondria, and it is the reason a plant stays alive, grows, repairs itself, and responds to its surroundings. In this process, glucose obtained from photosynthesis or stored food is oxidised so that the locked-up chemical energy is set free for use by the plant. The syllabus asks you to study two main types of respiration in plants. The first is aerobic respiration, which requires oxygen and can be written in a word equation as glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy. This happens in most plant cells when oxygen is freely available, such as in the leaves, stems and roots of ordinary terrestrial plants, and it releases a large amount of usable energy. The second is anaerobic respiration, which does not need oxygen and, in the familiar example of yeast fermentation, can be written as glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. In the absence of oxygen, such as in roots standing in waterlogged soil or in the microorganisms used in making Indian foods like idli or dosa batter, organisms switch to this less efficient pathway. Because anaerobic respiration is incomplete, it releases far less energy and often produces alcohol as a by-product. Students must learn to distinguish the two types clearly on the basis of oxygen requirement, the products formed and the amount of energy released. They should also remember that respiration is not the opposite of photosynthesis in every detail, but rather the complementary biochemical partner: photosynthesis builds glucose using sunlight, while respiration breaks glucose down to release energy. The importance of respiration for plant survival can hardly be overstated, because without it the plant would have no energy for absorbing mineral ions, for cell division, for opening and closing stomata, or for surviving periods of darkness. In short, respiration is the slow, controlled burning of fuel inside the plant that keeps the engine of life running.
eli5: Plants need energy to live, just like you. They make food sugar called glucose in their leaves, and then they break that sugar apart inside their cells to get energy. When there is plenty of air, they use oxygen to break the sugar fully into carbon dioxide and water, releasing lots of energy. When there is no air, like roots stuck in muddy water, they break the sugar partly into alcohol and a little energy. This breaking of food to release energy is called respiration.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration in plants and the word equation for anaerobic respiration as it occurs in yeast.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen, and its word equation is glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy. This means that one molecule of glucose reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy that the plant can use for growth, repair and other life processes. Anaerobic respiration in yeast, which is also called fermentation, is the breakdown of glucose without using oxygen, and its word equation is glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. In this case the sugar is not broken down completely, so the products include alcohol, also called ethanol, and carbon dioxide, but only a small amount of energy is released. The two equations should always be written with the reactants on the left side of the arrow and the products on the right side, and the word "energy" must not be left out because the release of energy is the whole point of respiration.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why do plants release carbon dioxide at night, even though they take in carbon dioxide during the day for photosynthesis?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Plants release carbon dioxide at night because respiration is a continuous process that goes on both during the day and during the night. In the daytime, the plant is both photosynthesising and respiring. Photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, while respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Usually the rate of photosynthesis during the day is higher than the rate of respiration, so the plant appears to take in carbon dioxide overall. At night, however, there is no sunlight, so photosynthesis stops, but respiration does not stop because the plant still needs energy to stay alive. Therefore the carbon dioxide produced by respiration is not used up by photosynthesis and diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata, making it seem as though the plant is releasing carbon dioxide only at night. This is one reason why it is wrong to say that plants respire only in the dark; they respire all the time, but the gas exchange is most noticeable at night.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Respiration in plants is just the reverse of photosynthesis, and plants do not need to respire because they can make their own food." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly based on a true observation but it is ultimately incorrect, and it confuses two different but complementary processes. It is true that photosynthesis and respiration are related: in photosynthesis, which takes place mainly in the leaves in the presence of sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are combined to form glucose and oxygen, so it is a building-up process that stores energy. In respiration, glucose is broken down, usually with oxygen, to release carbon dioxide, water and energy, so in terms of the raw materials and the products the two equations appear to run in opposite directions. However, saying they are simply reverse of one another ignores several important differences. Photosynthesis needs sunlight and chlorophyll and occurs only in green plant parts, whereas respiration occurs in all living cells of the plant at all times, with or without light. Moreover, the statement that plants do not need to respire because they make their own food is wrong. Making food through photosynthesis is not the same as using the food. The glucose produced by photosynthesis stores energy in its chemical bonds, but this energy is useless to the plant until it is released by respiration. Without respiration, the plant would have no energy to absorb water and minerals, to build new cells, to repair damaged tissues, to open and close stomata, or to respond to gravity and light. Therefore, photosynthesis and respiration are partners, not opposites, and respiration is absolutely essential for the plant's survival. A plant that could not respire would soon die, no matter how much food it had made.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A farmer in a rice-growing region of West Bengal notices that some paddy seedlings have turned yellow and wilted in a waterlogged field. Using your knowledge of respiration in plants, explain what type of respiration may be occurring in the roots and why the seedlings are in trouble.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In a waterlogged field the spaces between soil particles are filled with water, so the oxygen that normally diffuses into the soil is greatly reduced. Under these conditions the roots of the paddy seedlings cannot obtain enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, and they may switch to anaerobic respiration. In anaerobic respiration, glucose is only partly broken down, producing alcohol, also called ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy. The word equation is glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. The problem is that this process releases much less energy than aerobic respiration, so the roots do not get enough energy to absorb mineral salts and water from the soil effectively. Worse still, if alcohol accumulates in the root cells it can become toxic and damage the tissues. As a result, the roots cannot supply the rest of the plant with the water and minerals it needs, the leaves lose their turgidity and turn yellow, and the seedlings wilt. This is why farmers often drain waterlogged paddy fields for short periods or plant rice varieties that can tolerate low oxygen and send special breathing roots above the water surface.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple school-laboratory experiment to show that germinating seeds release carbon dioxide during respiration.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To show that germinating seeds release carbon dioxide, take two clean boiling tubes or small flasks. In the first, labelled A, place a small handful of germinating seeds, such as germinating gram or moong seeds that have been soaked overnight and kept moist in a warm place for a day. In the second, labelled B, place an equal quantity of boiled and cooled seeds as a control, so that the only difference between the two tubes is that the seeds in A are alive and respiring. Fit each tube with a one-hole stopper through which a bent delivery tube passes. The free end of each delivery tube should dip into a small beaker or test tube containing freshly prepared lime water, which is a clear solution of calcium hydroxide. Make the apparatus airtight and leave it undisturbed in a warm place for about fifteen to thirty minutes. After some time the lime water into which the delivery tube from tube A dips will turn milky, showing the presence of carbon dioxide, because the germinating seeds in A are respiring and producing carbon dioxide. The lime water in the control beaker connected to tube B will remain clear, because the boiled seeds are dead and cannot respire. The same test can be made more sensitive by keeping the tubes in a dark cupboard so that photosynthesis does not interfere if green seedlings are used, though with germinating seeds photosynthesis is not a major concern. This experiment proves that living, germinating seeds release carbon dioxide as a product of respiration.

masteryCriteria: Can write the word equation for respiration in plants (glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy); can state that respiration occurs in all plant parts; can distinguish between respiration and photosynthesis (respiration releases energy, photosynthesis stores energy).

title: Photosynthesis vs respiration
subject: bio
definition: Photosynthesis and respiration are two fundamental life processes that every Class 7 student must compare and contrast in the study of plant life. Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. It occurs mainly in the leaves, specifically inside the green chloroplasts that contain the pigment chlorophyll. The overall word equation is: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, produces glucose + oxygen. The chemical equation, which examiners often ask students to write, is 6CO2 + 6H2O, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, yielding C6H12O6 + 6O2. This is an anabolic, endothermic process because it stores light energy in the chemical bonds of glucose. Respiration, by contrast, is the catabolic, exothermic process by which all living cells break down glucose in the presence of oxygen to release carbon dioxide, water, and usable energy in the form of ATP. The word equation is: glucose + oxygen produces carbon dioxide + water + energy, and the chemical equation is C6H12O6 + 6O2 yielding 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. A good comparison table lists inputs and outputs, site of occurrence, energy change, gas exchange, and dependence on light. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, while respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide; hence they are opposite processes. Photosynthesis occurs only in the green parts of a plant during the daytime, because it needs light. Respiration occurs in all living cells, in plants and animals alike, continuously, both day and night. The two processes maintain the carbon dioxide-oxygen balance in nature. Green plants absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and release oxygen, while all organisms release carbon dioxide during respiration. This cycling keeps the atmospheric gases in a state of equilibrium, supporting life on Earth. Indian students can picture the paddy fields of West Bengal and the wheat fields of Punjab during bright summer days, where millions of leaves are performing photosynthesis, while at the same time all plant and animal cells are quietly respiring. Understanding this complementary relationship is essential not only for the board exam but also for understanding how ecosystems work.
eli5: Plants make their own food using sunlight, air, and water. This is called photosynthesis. It makes sugar and gives out oxygen. All living things use oxygen to break sugar and get energy to live. This is called respiration. It gives out carbon dioxide. So plants help make oxygen, and all of us help make carbon dioxide. They balance each other like a see-saw.

misconceptions.belief: Plants only respire at night and only photosynthesize during the day. This is a common error that appears in many student answers. The board examiner observations from 2025 note that candidates are often confused about the conditions and timing of photosynthesis. The correction is that photosynthesis occurs only during the daytime because it needs sunlight, but respiration occurs continuously, both day and night, in all living cells, because every cell needs energy all the time.

The products of photosynthesis are glucose and oxygen only, and water is sometimes missed. The board exam analysis examiner comment specifically states that "some missed one of the products, such as water, or wrote an unbalanced equation." The correction is that the complete outputs of photosynthesis are glucose and oxygen, and the complete inputs are carbon dioxide and water. If writing the equation, water must appear on the left side, and the equation must be balanced.

Photosynthesis and respiration are unrelated processes, with plants doing one and animals doing the other. This is not true. Plants perform both photosynthesis and respiration. Photosynthesis occurs only in green parts, while respiration occurs in all living cells of all organisms. The two processes are linked because the outputs of photosynthesis, glucose and oxygen, are the inputs of respiration, and the outputs of respiration, carbon dioxide and water, are inputs of photosynthesis. This link maintains the CO2-O2 balance in nature.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis and respiration.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The inputs of photosynthesis are carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight. Carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores called stomata in the leaves, water is absorbed from the soil by the roots and transported through the xylem, and sunlight is captured by the green pigment chlorophyll. The outputs of photosynthesis are glucose, which is food for the plant, and oxygen, which is released into the air. In respiration, the inputs are glucose and oxygen. The glucose is the same food molecule produced during photosynthesis or taken in through food in animals, and oxygen is taken from the air. The outputs of respiration are carbon dioxide, water, and energy. This energy is released in the mitochondria of cells and is used for all life processes such as growth, movement, and reproduction. Thus, the inputs of one process match the outputs of the other, creating a cycle of gas and energy exchange in living organisms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does respiration occur in all living cells continuously, while photosynthesis occurs only in green parts during the daytime?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Respiration occurs in all living cells continuously because every cell needs a constant supply of energy to stay alive. Whether it is a leaf cell, a root cell, or a human muscle cell, all cells must break down glucose to release energy, and this cannot stop even for a moment without harming the organism. Respiration does not depend on light, so it can proceed day and night. Photosynthesis, on the other hand, needs three things together: carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight energy. It also needs chlorophyll, the green pigment found in chloroplasts of green plant parts such as leaves. Without sunlight, the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis cannot take place, so it occurs only during the day. Since chlorophyll is absent in non-green parts like roots and most stems, those parts cannot photosynthesize at all. Therefore, the scope and timing of the two processes are very different, yet both are essential for life.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Plants produce oxygen during the day through photosynthesis, so at night they must stop making oxygen. This means plants stop respiring at night too." Is this statement correct? Evaluate with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly correct and partly incorrect, and a good student must separate the two parts. It is true that plants stop producing oxygen at night, because oxygen is produced only during photosynthesis, and photosynthesis requires sunlight. In the absence of light at night, photosynthesis stops, and therefore the plant stops releasing oxygen. However, the second part of the statement is wrong. Plants do not stop respiring at night. Respiration is a continuous process that takes place in all living cells, day and night, because cells need energy at all times. At night, the plant still takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, just like it does during the day. In fact, at night, only respiration is happening in plants, not photosynthesis, so the plant is a net producer of carbon dioxide and consumer of oxygen during those hours. During the day, the rate of photosynthesis is usually greater than the rate of respiration in a green leaf, so the plant appears to release more oxygen than carbon dioxide. But respiration never stops. Thus, the statement confuses the light-dependence of photosynthesis with the continuous nature of respiration.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Construct a balanced tabular comparison of photosynthesis and respiration for a board answer, covering inputs, outputs, site, energy change, gas exchange, and dependence on light.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A good tabular comparison for the board should be neat, complete, and directly related to the syllabus. The table should have two columns, one for photosynthesis and one for respiration. Under inputs, photosynthesis has carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight, while respiration has glucose and oxygen. Under outputs, photosynthesis produces glucose and oxygen, while respiration produces carbon dioxide, water, and energy. Under site of occurrence, photosynthesis occurs in green parts of plants, mainly in leaves with chloroplasts, while respiration occurs in all living cells of plants and animals. Under energy change, photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in glucose, while respiration releases chemical energy from glucose for use by the cell. Under gas exchange, photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, while respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Under dependence on light, photosynthesis requires sunlight and occurs only during the day, while respiration does not depend on light and occurs continuously, both day and night. Such a table scores full marks because it covers every point mentioned in the syllabus.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are a science teacher in a Class 7 classroom. Design a creative classroom demonstration or activity that helps students understand how photosynthesis and respiration maintain the CO2-O2 balance in nature.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A creative classroom activity could be the "Balanced Piggy Bank of Gases." The teacher divides the class into two groups: the Photosynthesis Group and the Respiration Group. The Photosynthesis Group, representing green leaves, holds green paper leaves and a bowl labeled "Sunlight Energy." They take in blue tokens representing carbon dioxide and clear tokens representing water, and they produce yellow tokens representing glucose and white tokens representing oxygen. The Respiration Group, representing all living cells, takes the yellow glucose tokens and white oxygen tokens and returns blue carbon dioxide tokens and clear water tokens back to the Photosynthesis Group. The teacher can then introduce a third group, the Atmosphere Group, which keeps a count of oxygen and carbon dioxide tokens. As the tokens circulate, the class sees that the number of oxygen and carbon dioxide tokens remains balanced. The teacher can also discuss how cutting down too many trees, such as the deforestation happening in parts of the Amazon or even in some Indian forests, would reduce the photosynthesis group and disturb the balance. This activity is memorable because it turns abstract gas cycles into a physical, visual, and participatory experience.

masteryCriteria: Can state three differences between photosynthesis and respiration (photosynthesis: produces food, uses CO2, needs sunlight; respiration: breaks down food, uses oxygen, occurs all the time); can explain why plants need both processes.

title: Excretory system
subject: bio
definition: The human excretory system, specifically the renal excretory system, is the organ system responsible for removing metabolic wastes and harmful substances from the bloodstream, thereby maintaining the body's internal balance. Its main organs are the two kidneys, a pair of bean-shaped organs located at the back of the abdomen, one on each side of the spine. Each kidney receives blood through the renal artery, and the blood is filtered inside millions of tiny working units called nephrons. During this filtration, waste products such as urea, excess salts, and extra water are removed from the blood while useful substances like glucose and most of the water are returned to the blood through reabsorption. The cleaned blood then leaves through the renal vein. The waste liquid formed by the kidneys is called urine. From each kidney, urine passes down a narrow muscular tube called the ureter to a muscular, balloon-like organ called the urinary bladder, which stores urine until it is expelled. When the bladder is full, the sphincter muscles relax, and urine travels out of the body through another tube called the urethra. In this way, the kidneys act like a water purifier: they remove dissolved nitrogenous waste and keep the blood composition stable. Common disorders of this system include urinary tract infection (UTI), usually caused by bacteria entering through the urethra and leading to pain, burning sensation, and frequent urination; and kidney stones, which are hard mineral and salt deposits that form inside the kidneys, causing severe pain, difficulty in passing urine, and sometimes blood in the urine. Basic prevention includes drinking adequate clean water, maintaining hygiene, and avoiding holding urine for too long. The term excretion refers to the whole process of removing these wastes from the body, and the renal system is essential for healthy blood, proper water balance, and overall well-being.
eli5: Your body makes waste when it digests food. The kidneys clean your blood by catching that waste and turning it into urine. The urine travels through tubes to a bag called the bladder. When the bladder gets full, you go to the toilet and the urine leaves through another tube. Drinking water and keeping clean helps the kidneys stay healthy.

misconceptions.belief: "Excretion just means passing urine." board examiners have observed that many candidates wrote answers like "passing urine" without explaining the role of the urinary bladder and sphincter muscles, and lost marks. The correction is that excretion is the entire process: the kidneys filter blood, the ureters carry urine, the bladder stores it, and the urethra removes it. Always name each organ and its role.

"Writing 'removal of wastes from the body' is enough for any excretory question." This vague wording does not earn full marks, as examiners noted when candidates lost marks for not including the specific organs and processes involved. The correction is to give a complete, specific answer, for example: "The kidneys filter blood to remove urea, excess salts, and water, forming urine, which is stored in the urinary bladder and passed out through the urethra."

"Only the kidney is involved in urination." Some students forget the ureter, bladder, and urethra and describe the process as a single step. The correction is to remember that the four organs work in sequence: kidneys filter, ureters transport, bladder stores, and urethra eliminates.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Name the four main parts of the renal excretory system and explain one major function of each in the correct order.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The four main parts of the renal excretory system are the kidneys, the ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra. The two kidneys are bean-shaped organs located at the back of the abdomen, one on each side of the spine. Their major function is to filter the blood and remove waste products such as urea, excess salts, and extra water to form urine. Inside the kidneys, tiny units called nephrons carry out the actual filtration, and useful substances such as glucose and most of the water are returned to the blood by reabsorption. The two ureters are narrow muscular tubes that carry the urine from the kidneys downward to the urinary bladder. The urinary bladder is a muscular, balloon-like organ that stores urine until it can be released; it stretches as it fills and its sphincter muscles keep the urine inside until you decide to pass it. Finally, the urethra is the tube through which urine leaves the body when the bladder is full and the sphincter muscles relax. Each part therefore has a distinct and sequential role in the formation, transport, storage, and removal of urine.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain how the kidneys help maintain the composition of blood while forming urine. Use the terms filtration and reabsorption in your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The kidneys maintain blood composition by continuously filtering the blood that enters them through the renal artery. As blood flows through the millions of nephrons inside the kidneys, waste substances such as urea, excess mineral salts, and surplus water are filtered out from the blood. However, the kidneys are selective and do not remove everything. Useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, and most of the water are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream through a process called reabsorption. This means that the kidneys remove harmful and unnecessary materials while keeping the valuable materials the body still needs. As a result, the blood leaving the kidneys through the renal vein is cleaner and better balanced, and the waste that is left behind is collected as urine. By this process, the kidneys regulate the amount of water and salts in the blood and prevent the build-up of toxic nitrogenous waste such as urea in the body.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Drinking a lot of water is a waste because the body only needs a small amount to make urine, and less water means less work for the kidneys." Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, and it shows a poor understanding of how the kidneys work. It is true that the body can produce urine even with a small amount of water, because the kidneys are designed to conserve water when the body is short of it. However, the claim that less water means less work for the kidneys is wrong. When a person drinks too little water, the urine becomes concentrated and contains a higher amount of dissolved salts and urea. This makes it easier for mineral crystals to clump together and form kidney stones. It also reduces the flushing action that normally helps remove bacteria from the urinary tract, increasing the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs). On the other hand, drinking adequate clean water keeps the urine dilute, which helps the kidneys filter waste efficiently and lowers the risk of stones and infections. Therefore, while the kidneys can manage with less water for short periods, the statement that drinking a lot of water is a waste is not correct. Good hydration is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect the excretory system. The balanced view is that the body needs enough water--not too little and not an extreme excess--to keep the kidneys healthy and the urine flowing smoothly, which is especially important in a hot and humid climate.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Ria often feels a burning sensation when she urinates and has a strong, frequent urge to pass very small amounts of urine. Her mother asks her what she should do. What condition might Ria have, what could have caused it, and what two practical steps should she take immediately?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Ria's symptoms--a burning sensation while urinating, a frequent urge to urinate, and passing only small amounts of urine--suggest that she may have a urinary tract infection (UTI). A UTI is usually caused by bacteria, commonly from the skin around the genital area or from unhygienic toilet conditions, entering the urethra and growing in the urinary tract. In hot and humid weather, sweating reduces the amount of water available for making urine, which makes it easier for bacteria to multiply. The two most practical steps she should take immediately are to drink plenty of clean, boiled or filtered water, which will help flush the bacteria out of the urinary system, and to keep the genital area clean and dry, wiping from front to back after using the toilet. She should also avoid holding urine for long periods and should consult a doctor, because a UTI often needs proper medical treatment. These simple habits can reduce both the discomfort and the chance of the infection returning.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a one-day school campaign for World Kidney Day to teach younger students how the kidneys work and how to keep them healthy. Plan at least two activities and two key messages.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the World Kidney Day campaign, the first key message would be "Kidneys are your body's natural water purifiers: they filter waste from the blood and make urine." The second key message would be "Drink enough clean water every day and keep yourself clean to protect your kidneys and urinary tract." The first activity could be a "Kidney Journey" display showing a large chart of the excretory system, with four labelled stations: Kidney (the filter), Ureter (the tube), Urinary Bladder (the storage tank), and Urethra (the exit). Younger students would move from station to station and collect a sticker at each one, learning the organ and its function. The second activity could be a "Water Challenge" in which each student keeps a simple log of how many glasses of water they drink in a day and receives a badge for meeting a healthy target. During the campaign, students could also prepare short slogans such as "Clean water, happy kidneys" and "Don't hold it--go!" These activities would reinforce the idea that the excretory system is a sequence of organs working together, and that good daily habits help prevent common problems such as UTIs and kidney stones.

masteryCriteria: Can name the main excretory organs (kidneys, skin, lungs, liver); can state the function of kidneys (filter blood, produce urine); can describe the path of urine formation (filtration in kidney -> ureter -> bladder -> urethra).

title: Nervous system parts
subject: bio
definition:
The nervous system is the body's rapid communication and control network. It is made up of three main parts: the brain, the spinal cord, and the nerves. All three work together so that the body can sense changes in the environment, think, decide, and respond quickly and in a coordinated way.

The brain is the largest part of the nervous system and sits safely inside the skull. It can be divided into three main parts, each with one important function. The cerebrum is the large, folded upper part of the brain. It is responsible for thinking, learning, memory, and all voluntary actions -- the movements we choose to make, such as writing, solving a mathematics problem, or kicking a football. The cerebellum lies at the back of the head, below the cerebrum. It keeps the body balanced and coordinates the movement of muscles, so that actions such as walking, running, dancing, or riding a bicycle are smooth and steady. The medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brain, where the brain joins the spinal cord. It controls many involuntary actions -- the actions that happen without our conscious thought -- such as breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, and reflexes like coughing or sneezing.

The spinal cord is a long, soft bundle of nerve tissue that runs from the base of the brain down through the vertebral column, the column of bones called vertebrae that form the backbone. Its main function is to carry messages between the brain and the rest of the body. Sensory messages travel upward from the body to the brain, telling the brain what is happening around the body. Motor messages travel downward from the brain to the muscles and glands, telling them what to do. The spinal cord also controls some simple reflex actions on its own, without waiting for instructions from the brain.

Nerves are the long, thread-like structures that branch out from the brain and spinal cord to all parts of the body. A nerve is not the same as a single neuron. A nerve is a bundle of many nerve fibres, which are the long parts, or axons, of many neurons grouped together and wrapped in protective coverings. Nerves carry impulses, or tiny electrical signals, to and from the brain and spinal cord. Sensory nerves bring impulses from sense organs and the rest of the body toward the central nervous system. Motor nerves carry impulses away from the brain and spinal cord to muscles and glands. Many nerves in the body, such as the spinal nerves, are mixed nerves because they contain both sensory and motor fibres. Because of this two-way traffic of impulses, the body can both receive information and send out instructions, allowing control, coordination, and quick response to everything that happens inside and outside the body.
eli5: Your body has a special message system. The brain is the boss that thinks and decides. The spinal cord is a long message road inside your backbone. Nerves are like tiny wires that carry messages between the brain, spinal cord, and body. Each part of the brain has its own job: thinking, balance, or breathing and heartbeat. This lets you move, feel, and stay safe.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Name the three main parts of the nervous system and the three main parts of the brain. State one function of each part of the brain.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The three main parts of the nervous system are the brain, the spinal cord, and the nerves. The brain is the main control centre that receives information, makes decisions, and sends commands. The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerve tissue running through the vertebral column and carries messages between the brain and the body. Nerves are branching bundles of nerve fibres that carry impulses to and from the brain and spinal cord. The three main parts of the brain are the cerebrum, the cerebellum, and the medulla oblongata. The cerebrum is the large upper part responsible for thinking, learning, memory, and voluntary actions such as writing and speaking. The cerebellum, found at the back of the brain, maintains body balance and coordinates the contraction of muscles so that movements are smooth and controlled. The medulla oblongata is the lower part of the brain that continues into the spinal cord and controls involuntary actions such as breathing, heartbeat, and reflexes like coughing and sneezing. Remembering these names and functions precisely is the foundation for every other question on this topic.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a nerve is called a bundle of nerve fibres and how it is different from a single neuron.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A nerve is called a bundle of nerve fibres because, when seen under a microscope, it looks like a thick cable made of many long, thread-like fibres grouped together and wrapped in protective layers. Each of these fibres is the axon of a single neuron. The neuron itself is the complete nerve cell. It has a cell body that contains the nucleus, short branches called dendrites that receive messages, and a long thin process called the axon, or nerve fibre, that carries the message away. One neuron by itself is a single cell, but in the body the axons of hundreds or thousands of neurons are bundled together to form a nerve. This bundling is useful because it allows thousands of messages to travel together between the central nervous system and the rest of the body. So the difference is simple but important: a neuron is the cell, and a nerve is a collection of many nerve fibres, or axons, from many neurons. If a question asks you what a nerve is, the answer should always mention "bundle of nerve fibres" and not just "a nerve cell" or "neuron."

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "The medulla oblongata is the most important part of the brain because it keeps us breathing and our heart beating, so we could not live without it." Do you agree or disagree? Give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is partly correct but not completely fair, because every main part of the brain has a special and necessary function. It is true that the medulla oblongata is extremely important. It controls involuntary actions such as breathing, heartbeat, and blood pressure, and these processes must continue all the time, even when we are asleep. If the medulla stopped working, life would quickly be in danger, so it is easy to see why someone might call it the most important. However, the cerebrum is also vital because it is the centre of thinking, memory, learning, and voluntary action. Without the cerebrum, a person could not read, write, speak, solve problems, or make decisions. The cerebellum is equally important because it maintains balance and coordinates the muscles. Without it, a person could not walk, stand, or even hold a pencil properly. Therefore, saying that one part is the most important is not a balanced scientific view. The brain works as a team: the cerebrum plans and decides, the cerebellum makes the movement steady and balanced, and the medulla keeps the life-supporting processes running automatically. Each part depends on the others, and all three are essential for normal life.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine a student in India is learning to ride a bicycle on a narrow, uneven village lane. Describe the role of the cerebellum, the spinal cord, and the nerves in helping the student maintain balance and keep pedalling safely.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When the student is riding the bicycle, many parts of the nervous system work together. The eyes and inner ear send messages about the position of the body and the road surface through sensory nerves. These messages travel along the spinal cord up to the cerebellum. The cerebellum then compares the information about balance and movement and sends instructions to the muscles of the legs, arms, and back so that the student can sit upright and adjust to bumps. If the bicycle suddenly tilts to one side, the cerebellum quickly tells the muscles on the opposite side to contract and keep the balance. At the same time, the spinal cord is carrying messages between the brain and the rest of the body. Some fine adjustments, such as changing the pressure on the handlebars or the pedals, are partly controlled through nerves that carry impulses from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles. The mixed nerves in the arms and legs contain both sensory and motor fibres, so they can bring information in and send commands out. In this way, the cerebellum provides balance and coordination, the spinal cord acts as the message highway, and the nerves deliver the signals that allow the student to ride the bicycle safely and smoothly.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple poster for a Class 7 science exhibition that shows the three main parts of the brain and the three main parts of the nervous system. Describe the labels and the one-line messages you would include.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The poster would have a large central drawing of the human head and backbone with three clear sections. At the top, the brain would be shown with its three parts colour-coded: the cerebrum in blue, the cerebellum in green, and the medulla oblongata in red. Below the brain, the spinal cord would be drawn as a thick yellow column running through the vertebral column. Branching out from the spinal cord, thin red and blue lines would represent the nerves spreading to the arms, legs, and other organs. Each part would have a one-line label: "Cerebrum -- the thinking and learning part," "Cerebellum -- keeps you balanced and your movements smooth," and "Medulla oblongata -- controls breathing and heartbeat automatically." The spinal cord would be labelled, "Message highway between brain and body." The nerves would be labelled, "Bundles of nerve fibres that carry impulses to and from the brain and spinal cord." At the bottom, a slogan would read, "Nervous System: The Body's Control and Communication Network." The poster would help visitors quickly understand that the brain, spinal cord, and nerves are the three main parts and that each part of the brain has one major function.

masteryCriteria: Can name the three main parts of the nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves); can state the function of the brain (control and coordination), spinal cord (reflex actions), and nerves (carry signals); can define a reflex action with one example (touching hot object).

title: Allergy concept and allergens
subject: bio
definition: An allergy is a condition in which the body's immune system overreacts to substances that are normally harmless to most people. In simple terms, the immune system, which is the body's defence army, treats an ordinary substance as if it were a dangerous enemy. This false alarm causes reactions such as sneezing, coughing, runny nose, watering eyes, skin rash, or itching. The substance that causes this reaction is called an allergen. Allergens are not germs, and they do not cause infections, but the body mistakenly identifies them as threats and releases chemicals like histamine, which produces the uncomfortable symptoms of an allergy. Common allergens in the environment around us include dust, tiny particles called pollen grains that come from flowers and grasses, dust mites, strong sunlight, and certain food items such as shellfish and nuts. Each allergen can enter the body through different routes. When a person eats something he or she is sensitive to, the allergen enters through the mouth. When dust or pollen floats in the air and is breathed in, it enters through the nose. When the skin touches something irritating, such as certain plants, fabrics, or chemicals, the allergen enters through the skin. It is important to understand the difference between an allergen and an allergy. The allergen is the trigger, the thing that starts the problem. The allergy is the body's response, the set of symptoms that appear after contact with the allergen. For example, dust is the allergen, but sneezing and a runny nose are the allergy. Pollen is the allergen, but watering eyes and sneezing are the allergy. Food such as shellfish is the allergen, but a rash or stomach discomfort is the allergy. In Indian contexts, children may come across dust from old books in school libraries, pollen from neem or parthenium plants in neighbourhoods, dust mites in bedding and carpets, and strong sunlight during outdoor activities in summer. Sensitivity to particular food items, such as peanuts, cashew nuts, or prawns, is also commonly observed. The concept of histamine helps explain why the symptoms appear: when the immune system detects an allergen, it releases histamine, which makes the blood vessels widen and causes swelling, itching, and other signs of an allergic reaction. Therefore, learning about allergy means understanding the role of the immune system, the examples of allergens, the entry routes through the nose, mouth, and skin, and the clear distinction between the trigger and the reaction.
eli5: An allergy is when your body gets too worried about something that is not really dangerous, like dust or a nut. It sends a false alarm, and then you sneeze, cough, or get a rash. The thing that sets off the alarm is called an allergen. Allergens can come into your body through your mouth, nose, or skin.

misconceptions.belief: Students often think an allergy is the same as an allergen. The board examiner observations show that students can be confused by similar-sounding terms. For example, in the board exam analysis data, candidates mixed up GDP and GNP because the names looked alike, and in the same way, children sometimes write "allergy" when they mean "allergen.
misconceptions.correction: an allergen is the trigger substance; an allergy is the body's reaction to that substance. Dust is the allergen, but sneezing is the allergy.

misconceptions.belief: Some students think all allergies are caused by germs, because they remember from Class 6 that diseases are caused by pathogens. This is not true for allergies.
misconceptions.correction: an allergy is an overreaction of the immune system to harmless substances such as pollen, dust, or food. It is not an infection, and it is not spread from person to person.

misconceptions.belief: Students sometimes list any pollutant as a trigger of allergy, similar to how candidates in the board exam analysis incorrectly wrote "smoke" and "haze" as air pollutants when they were not the expected answers. Smoke may irritate the nose, but it is not the same as an allergen.
misconceptions.correction: common allergens for this syllabus are dust, pollen grains, dust mites, strong sunlight, and particular food items such as shellfish and nuts.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define allergy and give any four common examples of allergens.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Allergy is an overreaction of the body's immune system to substances that are normally harmless. In other words, the immune system mistakes a harmless substance for a dangerous enemy and releases chemicals such as histamine, which cause symptoms like sneezing, runny nose, watering eyes, itching, or skin rash. An allergen is the substance that triggers this reaction. Four common examples of allergens are dust, pollen grains, dust mites, and particular food items such as shellfish and nuts. Dust is present in homes, schools, and libraries, especially on old books and curtains. Pollen grains are tiny particles released by flowers and grasses; they float in the air and can be inhaled through the nose. Dust mites are microscopic organisms that live in dust, mattresses, carpets, and upholstery. Shellfish and nuts such as peanuts and cashew nuts can cause allergic reactions when eaten by sensitive people. Other examples include strong sunlight, which can affect the skin, and animal dander. To score well, the definition should clearly say that the body's immune system is reacting to a harmless substance, and the examples should be drawn from the syllabus list.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain the difference between an allergen and an allergy, using one example from each of the three entry routes: mouth, nose, and skin.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: An allergen is the substance that causes an allergic reaction, while an allergy is the body's response to that substance. The allergen is the cause or trigger; the allergy is the effect or set of symptoms. For the mouth, the allergen is a particular food item such as a peanut or shellfish, and the allergy is the stomach discomfort or skin rash that appears after eating it. For the nose, the allergen is dust or pollen grains floating in the air, and the allergy is sneezing, a runny nose, and watering eyes. For the skin, the allergen may be strong sunlight, a chemical in soap, or contact with a plant, and the allergy is a red, itchy rash or irritation on the skin. It is important not to mix the two terms in the examination. If the question asks for an allergen, the correct answer should name the trigger, such as "dust" or "pollen." If the question asks for an allergy, the correct answer should describe the reaction, such as "sneezing" or "skin rash." Using the terms correctly shows that the student has understood the distinction between the cause and the effect.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Pollen is a harmful substance because it causes allergies in many people." Do you agree with this statement? Give reasons for your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true but not completely correct, so it should be evaluated carefully. It is true that pollen can cause allergic reactions in some people. When a sensitive person inhales pollen grains through the nose, the immune system may overreact and release histamine, leading to sneezing, runny nose, and watering eyes. In this sense, pollen is an allergen for those people. However, pollen is not a harmful or dangerous substance in itself. It is a natural, harmless, and even useful part of the environment. Pollen is produced by flowers and is essential for plant reproduction because it helps in the process of pollination. Without pollen, many plants would not be able to produce seeds and fruits. For most people, pollen does not cause any problem at all. Only individuals who have a sensitivity or an overactive immune response to pollen experience allergies. Therefore, it would be wrong to say that pollen is harmful in general. It is more accurate to say that pollen is a harmless substance that triggers an allergic reaction in certain sensitive individuals. This is the key idea of the chapter: the immune system can overreact to normally harmless substances, and the substance itself is not the enemy. A balanced answer should accept the link between pollen and allergy, but also explain that pollen is not harmful by nature and plays a useful role in the life of plants.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Rina starts sneezing and her eyes begin to water whenever she sits near the open window during the spring mornings. She also gets a red rash on her skin when she eats prawns. Identify the likely allergens and the entry routes in each case. Suggest simple precautions she could take.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In the first situation, when Rina sits near the open window during spring mornings and starts sneezing with watering eyes, the likely allergen is pollen. In spring, many flowers and grasses release pollen grains into the air. The pollen enters Rina's body through the nose, which is the inhalation or nasal route. In the second situation, the red rash on her skin after eating prawns is caused by shellfish, which is a food allergen. The prawn allergen enters through the mouth, which is the ingestion or oral route, and the reaction appears on the skin as a rash. To reduce the pollen allergy, Rina could keep the windows closed during early morning hours, use a clean handkerchief, avoid going to grassy or flowering areas during high pollen times, and wash her face and hands after being outdoors. For the food allergy, she should avoid eating prawns and other shellfish, read food labels when eating outside, and inform her family and school about her sensitivity so that she is not served shellfish accidentally. These precautions target the entry routes: avoiding inhalation of pollen and avoiding ingestion of shellfish.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a small poster or chart for your school health club titled "Know Your Allergens." What information and pictures would you include, and how would you explain the three entry routes clearly to younger students?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The poster "Know Your Allergens" should have a bold title at the top and a friendly, colourful layout. In the first section, I would define allergy in simple terms: "An allergy is a false alarm in the body. The immune system thinks a harmless thing is dangerous and makes us sneeze, cough, or get a rash." The second section would show common allergens with pictures: a cloud of dust near old books, tiny pollen grains floating in the air, dust mites under a magnifying glass, a sun symbol for strong sunlight, and pictures of shellfish and nuts such as peanuts. The third section would clearly explain the three entry routes using labelled diagrams. For the mouth, I would draw a child eating a peanut with a cross over it and the words: "Food allergens enter through the mouth." For the nose, I would draw a child breathing in pollen or dust with the words: "Dust and pollen enter through the nose." For the skin, I would draw a hand touching sunlight and a plant with the words: "Sunlight and touch allergens enter through the skin." I would also include a "Good vs Bad" example box showing: "Good: Shellfish is the allergen, and the skin rash is the allergy." and "Bad: Allergy and allergen mean the same thing." At the bottom, I would add a safety tip: "If you often sneeze, cough, or get a rash, tell a parent, teacher, or doctor." This poster would help younger students remember the definition, the examples, and the three entry routes visually and clearly.

masteryCriteria: Can define allergy as an overreaction of the immune system; can name three common allergens (dust, pollen, food); can state two symptoms of an allergic reaction (sneezing, rash, itching).

title: Types of allergies and precautions
subject: bio
definition:
An allergy is a hypersensitive or exaggerated response of the body's immune system to a substance that is usually harmless to most people. The triggering substance is called an allergen. In Class 6, you learned that hygiene and sanitation keep disease-causing germs away; in Class 7, you now learn that even non-living or non-infectious particles such as pollen, dust, or animal dander can provoke a reaction because the body mistakes them for dangerous invaders. The symptoms of an allergic reaction are the body's way of warning you that it has detected such a substance. Common symptoms include repeated sneezing, itching of the skin or eyes, red or raised skin rashes, watering eyes, difficulty in breathing, and swelling of the face, lips, or other body parts. These symptoms are produced when the immune system releases chemicals such as histamine, and the word antihistamine is used for medicines that help reduce these symptoms.

Allergies are usually grouped by the time pattern of their appearance. A seasonal allergy appears at a particular time of the year. In India, spring, which falls roughly from February to April, brings an increase in pollen from grasses, flowering trees such as gulmohar, and cultivated crops. Hay fever is a well-known seasonal allergy in which the nose, eyes, and throat are irritated by this pollen. A perennial allergy, on the other hand, is present throughout the year because its cause is not tied to a season. The dust mite is a tiny arachnid that lives in house dust, mattresses, carpets, curtains, and soft toys, especially in warm and humid places such as coastal cities. Because dust mites are always present indoors, a dust mite allergy gives symptoms all year. Some children may also react to mould, pet dander, or cockroach droppings, and these can behave as perennial triggers as well.

The care of an allergy-prone person focuses on exposure, prevention, avoidance, and treatment. The most important precaution is avoidance of the known allergen. If pollen is the trigger, the person should keep windows closed during the pollen season, wear a protective mask while going outdoors, avoid morning walks through fields or gardens, and shower after coming home to wash off pollen. If dust mites are the trigger, the person should keep surroundings clean and dust-free, wash bed linen in hot water, use dust-proof covers on pillows and mattresses, and remove heavy curtains and carpets. Avoiding self-medication is essential; a person must consult a doctor, who may prescribe antihistamines or other medicines based on the exact cause and severity. The combination of avoidance and medical care gives the best prevention and treatment of allergic reactions.
eli5: Imagine your body is a guard who sometimes mistakes a friendly visitor for a robber. When pollen or dust enters, the guard makes you sneeze, itch, or get rashes to push the visitor out. Some visitors, like spring pollen, come only at a special time; others, like dust mites in your bed, stay all year. If you learn who the visitor is, you can avoid it or wear a mask, and a doctor can give medicine.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the common symptoms of an allergic reaction and give one example of a seasonal allergy and one example of a perennial allergy.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The common symptoms of an allergic reaction are the body's alarm signals when it meets an allergen. They include repeated sneezing, itching of the skin or eyes, red or raised skin rashes, watering eyes, difficulty in breathing, and swelling of parts of the face or body. These symptoms are caused by the release of chemicals such as histamine, which is why a doctor may sometimes give an antihistamine to reduce them. A seasonal allergy is one that appears at a particular time of the year; the best example is hay fever, which is caused by pollen in the spring when grasses and flowering trees release grains into the air. A perennial allergy is one that occurs throughout the year because its trigger is always present; the best example is dust mite allergy, in which a tiny creature living in house dust, mattresses, and carpets causes sneezing and itching all year round, especially in warm and humid homes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student in Class 7 says, "My friend sneezes a lot in February and March, but another friend sneezes even in July and December." Explain why one friend may have a seasonal allergy and the other a perennial allergy.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The friend who sneezes mainly in February and March is probably reacting to a seasonal trigger. In spring, trees and grasses release large amounts of pollen into the air, so a child with a pollen or hay fever allergy will show symptoms only when the pollen is present. Once the season ends, the symptoms usually disappear. The friend who sneezes even in July and December is probably reacting to a trigger that is present all year. Dust mites, for example, live in mattresses, pillows, carpets, and soft toys, and they do not vanish with the seasons. A dust mite allergy is therefore called a perennial allergy because it continues throughout the year. The key difference is not the symptom, but the time pattern of exposure to the allergen.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Antihistamine tablets are the best way to manage allergies, so children who have allergies do not need to avoid pollen or dust." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly true in one respect but wrong overall, so it must be evaluated carefully. It is true that antihistamines are useful medicines that help reduce symptoms such as sneezing, itching, and watering eyes by blocking the action of histamine in the body. They can make an allergic child feel much better during a bad attack. However, it is wrong to say that they are the best or only way to manage allergies, and it is also wrong to say that children do not need to avoid pollen or dust. Antihistamines do not cure the allergy; they only control the symptoms for a short time. If the child continues to breathe in pollen or sleep on a dust-filled pillow, the symptoms will return as soon as the medicine wears off. The most important long-term management is avoidance of the known allergen, which means keeping windows closed during pollen season, wearing protective masks, keeping the room clean and dust-free, and reducing exposure to dust mites.
